title: Ra and the creation of the world (Egypt)
subtitle: The creator sun
subject: mythologie
description: Ra, the sun god of Egypt: he creates the world, crosses the sky each day, fights chaos at night, and punishes humanity with his Eye.

hero.hook: Every dawn is a victory. Without the boat of Ra, the world would fall back into nothing.

blocks.text: **Ra** (or Re) is not only the sun. For the Egyptians of **Heliopolis**, the city of the solar cult near modern Cairo, he is the very principle of existence: he creates the world, then defends it every night against nothingness.

For three thousand years his figure runs through the state religion. To understand Ra is to understand how Egypt thought about the birth of the universe, the fragility of order, and why every dawn is a victory that has to be won again.

sections.title: How the world emerged: the primordial mound

blocks.text: Before time there is **Nun**: dark water, endless, full of seeds. The [[Heliopolitan cosmogony]] describes the appearance of **Atum**, “the one who is complete.” He fathers himself and rises on the **Benben Stone**, the first solid point.

blocks.caption: Atum rises from Nun on the Benben Stone

blocks.text: At Heliopolis the priests kept a sacred bird, the **Bennu** (ancestor of the phoenix), said to be the soul of Ra and to land on the Benben to announce a new cycle.

Alone, Atum creates **Shu** (air) and **Tefnut** (moisture), then **Geb** (Earth) and **Nut** (Sky), held apart to leave room for life. Then come **Osiris**, **Isis**, **Set** and **Nephthys**: with Atum, the **great Ennead**, the nine. [[Egyptian divine syncretism]] would later merge Atum and Ra into a single creator figure.

sections.title: Maat against Isfet: the perilous voyage of the boat

blocks.text: By day Ra sails in the boat **Mandjet**. At dusk he moves to the **Mesektet** and crosses the twelve hours of the [[Duat]], the world of the dead. This is not rest: it is a war against **Isfet**, disorder.

blocks.caption: The solar boat of Ra, the daily engine of time

blocks.text: From the 4th Dynasty on, almost every pharaoh carried “Ra” in his name: they called themselves “sons of Ra,” guarantors of the solar cycle.

The serpent **Apophis** tries to capsize the boat or to drink the waters of the heavenly Nile. **Set** himself sometimes defends the prow. When Ra is reborn at dawn as **Khepri**, the scarab, it is **Maat** (balance) that wins once more. An eclipse? Apophis almost won.

sections.title: The revolt of mankind and the destroying Eye

blocks.text: Even Ra grows old. In the story of “The Destruction of Mankind,” his bones turn to silver and humanity plots against him. Offended, he unleashes his burning Eye: the goddess [[Sekhmet]], a bloodthirsty lioness.

blocks.caption: Sekhmet, the Eye of Ra, before she becomes Hathor again

blocks.text: The slaughter threatens to put out creation itself. Ra has thousands of jars of beer brewed and dyed with red ocher, then poured over the fields. Sekhmet, believing she is drinking blood, gets drunk and calms down: she becomes gentle **Hathor**. The myth explains evil, and it justifies the festival of drunkenness, where people drank to celebrate the rescue of mankind.

sections.title: Legacy and fusion: the Amun-Ra version

blocks.text: In the New Kingdom the Theban god **Amun** merges with Ra, and **Amun-Ra** is born, “King of the Gods,” invisible creator and visible sun. The largest sanctuaries rise for him, such as [[Karnak Temple]].

Pyramids and obelisks turn the rays of the sun into stone to lift the pharaoh toward his heavenly father. Even the reform of **Akhenaten**, who imposed the cult of **Aten** (the disk), pushed an already solar idea to its limit. Ra remains the unmatched symbol of Egyptian stability.

**Ra** creates the world from Heliopolis, defends it every night in his boat against **Apophis**, and punishes then saves humanity through the Eye, **Sekhmet**. As **Amun-Ra**, he reigns at the summit of pharaonic Egypt.
